questions.stem: Your interpretation panel for a conference-history wing asks why the 1954 Geneva settlement ended the first Indochina war yet left the country divided. Explain the mechanism by which an end to fighting produced a divided state.

answer.exemplar: Geneva produced a temporary ceasefire that divided the country near the seventeenth parallel and required a wider conference to discuss political reunification. Because the sponsors set a time limit of two years for elections and reunification, and no strong authority was able to enforce the terms, fighting restarted in 1957 and the division hardened into two states.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why territorial sovereignty preceded economic development.
questions.stem: A curator asks you to explain why newly independent Asian and African states treated sovereignty over territory as the central issue rather than economic development at the 1955 gathering.

answer.exemplar: For states that had just won independence, control of territory was the precondition for everything else: without a government able to legislate, levy taxes and maintain order, development plans had no institution to carry them. Leaders who had been colonised also understood that formal equality without territorial authority was a legal fiction, so the conference made non-interference and self-determination the cornerstones of a new international order.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the 1956 operation could not be sustained.
questions.stem: A defence college lecturer asks why Britain and France could not sustain their 1956 operation against Egypt. Which reason is most accurate?

options.text: Their troops were defeated in a decisive field battle by much larger Egyptian forces.
options.misconception: invents a decisive Egyptian field victory over the invaders

options.text: Their forces lacked fuel and ammunition for more than a few days of operations.
options.misconception: invents a critical shortage of fuel and ammunition

options.text: The canal was permanently blocked by sunken ships that could not be removed.
options.misconception: invents a permanent blockage of the canal by sunken vessels

options.text: Other powers refused to support them, and domestic opinion turned against the move.

questions.explanation: The operation failed because external support evaporated and domestic opinion hardened against it, while the military outcome was indecisive. There was no decisive Egyptian victory, and the canal reopened.
questions.hint: Distinguish the military outcome from the political one.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Infer the economic basis of demands for constitutional reform.
questions.stem: An economics teaching sheet notes that colonial India ran a large share of its imports through British firms, that a large share of government revenue came from land taxes, and that the railway network ran from inland producers to coastal export terminals. What does the combination suggest?

options.text: Indian members had a strong economic argument that reform served imperial, not Indian, interests.
Indian members had no economic stake in how the empire's commercial system operated.
options.misconception: ignores the economic interests the figures reveal

options.text: The figures show that imperial trade policy had no effect on Indian incomes at all.
options.misconception: claims imperial trade policy left Indian incomes unaffected

options.text: The figures show that land taxes were a minor part of state revenue in the colony.
options.misconception: contradicts the stated share of revenue from land taxes

questions.explanation: Concentrated trade channels and heavy land taxation show that empire policy shaped Indian incomes, the economic basis of demands for reform. The figures show no indifference, and land taxes were a major revenue source.
questions.hint: Ask what the figures say about who benefited.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why partition left long-lasting administrative problems.
questions.stem: Your public history piece must explain why partition left the new states with administrative and fiscal problems that outlived the immediate violence.

answer.exemplar: The border cut across revenue systems, courts, police networks and irrigation works that had been built over generations, and the new governments inherited two sets of staff, two budgets and two legal codes operating in the same territory. Where communities had already fled, the officials, records and tax rolls they had left behind made it hard to know who owed what to whom. Recovery therefore meant rebuilding shared machinery while also handling the displacement of millions of people.

questions.explanation: Cutting shared institutions in two left duplicated authority, unclear obligations and damaged services that outlived the killing. The violence was the immediate shock; the administrative inheritance was the longer problem.
questions.hint: Think about what the new governments inherited in pieces.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Characterise popular support for the new republic from a diary entry.

stimulus.body: The people in this village ask only two things: that our children be taught in our own language and that the harvest tax be the same for everyone, whether they live on this side of the border or the other. They say the flag is welcome, provided the officials who come with it are people we recognise.

questions.stem: A curator uses this diary entry to characterise popular support for the new republic. Which conclusion does the entry best support?

options.text: The villagers demanded complete political independence from the Dutch and refused all officials.
options.misconception: reads the entry as a demand for rejecting outside officials

options.text: The villagers supported national authority but attached it to local identity and fair taxation.
The villagers were indifferent to the new state and cared only about the harvest tax.
options.misconception: reads the entry as showing indifference to the new state

options.text: The villagers opposed the republic because they feared new taxes on their harvest.
options.misconception: reads the entry as opposition to taxation by the new state

questions.explanation: The villagers welcome the national flag while insisting on language, equal tax and recognisable officials, which is conditional support rooted in local concerns. They rejected neither officials nor the state, and wanted fair tax.
questions.hint: Notice the conditions the villagers attach to their welcome.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why mass parties transformed decolonisation.
questions.stem: A tutor asks you to explain why the emergence of mass political parties was a decisive development for decolonisation in the Gold Coast. Which reasoning is best?

options.text: Parties turned scattered grievance into sustained pressure with a programme leaders could be judged on.
Parties replaced the need for negotiation by taking power directly from the colonial state.
options.misconception: claims parties made negotiation unnecessary

options.text: Parties existed in most colonies, so their emergence was not distinctive to the Gold Coast.
options.misconception: claims parties were already present in every colony

options.text: Parties prevented any violence, so the transition took place without disturbance of any kind.
options.misconception: claims parties removed the risk of disturbance

questions.explanation: Organised parties gave grievances a common programme, machinery and accountable leaders, turning scattered protests into negotiable pressure. They did not seize power directly, and the transition saw disturbance.
questions.hint: Focus on how parties changed the pressure on rulers.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an unbinding conference changed later bargaining.
questions.stem: A student assignment asks you to explain how a conference without a binding constitution could still change how states behaved in later negotiations with colonial powers.

answer.exemplar: The 1955 gathering produced a common set of principles that delegations could quote back to colonial governments: self-determination, refusal of outside interference and the claim that raw materials belonged to the people who lived on the ground. Because those principles were endorsed by many governments at once, a colonial official could no longer treat a demand from one state as the private grievance of a handful of dissidents, and had to answer a shared position rather than a single petitioner.

questions.explanation: Agreed principles let delegations speak with collective weight and turned private grievances into a shared position, so colonial officials had to answer a bloc. No binding text was needed for that effect.
questions.hint: Focus on how shared language changes bargaining leverage.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Infer how a boundary award distributed resources and communities.

stimulus.body: In the northern districts the award places the river, the railway line and the main market town on the western side of the boundary, while the eastern districts lose the headwaters that supplied their irrigation canals. The award adds that the line follows the watershed of the hills rather than the pattern of population.

questions.stem: An interpretive panel quotes this award. Which conclusion about how the border was drawn does it best support?

options.text: The border followed existing population patterns, so communities stayed together on both sides.
options.misconception: reads the award as following population patterns

options.text: The border followed physical features, splitting communities and leaving resources behind.
The border was drawn to distribute irrigation equally between the two new states.
options.misconception: reads the award as equalising access to irrigation

options.text: The border was drawn to place every important town and line inside one state.
options.misconception: reads the award as securing every town for one side

questions.explanation: The award names watershed and physical features as the basis for the line and shows assets left on one side, so communities and resources were split. Population patterns were not followed, and irrigation was not equalised.
questions.hint: Compare the stated criterion with what it produced.
